articles.title: Spain's Data Authority Receives First Breach Report Attributing an Attack to an AI Agent
articles.excerpt: An organisation has told Spain's data protection authority that an attacker used an AI agent to gain access to its system, modify personal information and access invoices. The Agencia Española de Prot…
articles.body: An organisation has told Spain's data protection authority that an attacker used an AI agent to gain access to its system, modify personal information and access invoices. The Agencia Española de Protección de Datos (AEPD) announced the notification on 14 September 2026. It was the first breach notification the agency had received in which "the incident would have been executed by means of an artificial intelligence agent that used a well-known language model." The account still required analysis, and the agency did not identify the organisation or the AI model involved. The reported sequence is the important part of this AI agent data breach: the agent searched for weaknesses, gained access and continued looking for ways to act inside the application.
articles.author: Jeanclaude Aoun

articles.body: Originally published in TL;JP , a weekly, fact-checked read on what Japanese AI and tech practitioners are saying on X. This is the Oct 6-12, 2026 issue. The posts I picked this week weren't about model scores. They were about nerve, method, and who gets to decide. 1. "AI can't do that" is mostly a question of nerve @mizchi argues that most claims of the form "AI can't do X" come down to kakugo — willingness to commit. They note that as recently as 2024, the mainstream position was that giving an AI access to bash was unthinkable, and that anyone who has felt how convenient Claude Code is can't go back. Security concerns, they say, end up ignored in the face of the convenience sitting right in front of you. That's their read, not a measurement.

articles.title: A headless CMS that only gives you an API is only half a product
articles.excerpt: This is how most headless CMS projects go for me. I pick a tool, set up my content models, and get an API. Nice. Then I sit down to build the actual app. List screen. Detail screen. A form with valida…
articles.body: This is how most headless CMS projects go for me. I pick a tool, set up my content models, and get an API. Nice. Then I sit down to build the actual app. List screen. Detail screen. A form with validation. Loading states, error states, empty states, search, pagination, login. Then I do it all again for the next model, and again on the next project. It’s the same twenty screens every time, and the API didn’t help with any of them. For years I built apps for small businesses, and almost every one needed the same things: a list of records, a detail page, an add/edit form and a login. Different clients, different logos, same screens. I must have built that set well over a dozen times before it finally annoyed me enough to do something about it. “Why not just reuse your code?” I did.

articles.body: I built a 17-agent AI swarm on my phone — here's how Okay, buckle up. This is going to be a bit of a deep dive. For the last few weeks, I’ve been obsessed with running a multi-agent system (a "swarm") directly on my phone. Not just accessing it remotely, but actually running the processing locally. And not just a few simple agents, but 17 interacting, goal-oriented AI entities. Why? Because it's cool, challenging, and I believe local AI processing is the future. Here's how I did it. The Vision: Decentralized Intelligence in Your Pocket I've been following the advancements in Large Language Models (LLMs) and agent frameworks with excitement. The idea of autonomous agents tackling complex tasks is incredibly powerful. However, much of the focus is on cloud-based solutions.
articles.author: Samuel James Hiotis

articles.title: The Real-Time AI Latency Budget, Allocated
articles.excerpt: Most latency targets for AI features arrive as one number on a ticket: "under 200 ms." Nobody owns 200 ms. Someone owns the vector search, someone owns the model server, someone owns the network in be…
articles.body: Most latency targets for AI features arrive as one number on a ticket: "under 200 ms." Nobody owns 200 ms. Someone owns the vector search, someone owns the model server, someone owns the network in between, and each of them assumes they get most of it. Below is the budget I'd start from for a retrieval-backed AI endpoint. A query comes in, relevant items are retrieved, a model ranks or scores them, and the result goes back while the user waits. Semantic search, recommendations and RAG-style lookups all have roughly this shape. Copy it, adjust it to your stack, and argue about it in the design review, not the incident review.
articles.author: Parikshit Talesara

articles.title: Is the LinkedIn API free? Pricing and posting access in 2026
articles.excerpt: LinkedIn charges nothing per API call, but posting to a company page takes its approval. Posting to your own profile is self-serve. Company pages need the Community Management API, which LinkedIn gran…
articles.body: LinkedIn charges nothing per API call, but posting to a company page takes its approval. Posting to your own profile is self-serve. Company pages need the Community Management API, which LinkedIn grants only to registered companies after a review, and which starts with a cap of 500 calls a day for the whole app. How much does the LinkedIn API cost? Nothing per call. LinkedIn's developer documentation describes access tiers and reviews, with no price list and no paid plan that buys more. What you do pay is a review before you can post to a company page, a daily cap while you are in the first tier, and upkeep: the API version you send expires, and so does every connection, once a year.
articles.author: Francisco José Fernández

articles.title: What Is Event Loop Lag in Node.js? How to Measure It (Part 1)
articles.excerpt: Your Node.js API gets slow. The database looks fine. So do the downstream services. Yet p99 latency has tripled and even the health check takes 300ms. Often the problem is the event loop itself. Node…
articles.body: Your Node.js API gets slow. The database looks fine. So do the downstream services. Yet p99 latency has tripled and even the health check takes 300ms. Often the problem is the event loop itself. Node runs your JavaScript on one thread, and when something keeps that thread busy, every other request in the process waits in line. That includes the ones that do almost nothing. That wait is called event loop lag . It's one of the cheapest metrics you can add to a Node service, and one of the most useful. This is part 1 of a 3-part series: What lag is, how to measure it, and when to check it (this post) The common causes and how to fix them CPU throttling: the lag your dashboard hides Every number below comes from scripts I ran on Node 22 in a 4 vCPU Linux container.

articles.title: The great Halley's Comet disappointment of 1986 — and the discoveries that changed astronomy forever
articles.excerpt: What disappointed skywatchers in 1986 became a scientific triumph, as an international fleet of spacecraft revealed the secrets of the world's most famous comet.
articles.body: This year, 2026, marks the 40th anniversary of the most recent appearance of Halley's Comet, the most famous comet in the solar system. Roughly every 76 years, Halley punctuates history like an exclamation mark in the night sky. As writer Guy Ottewell has said, it is the "wildest of the tame comets." It is a tame comet because it can be anticipated. It is wild because it is still fresh and bright; the brightest of all the recurring comets. It is the only one that periodically becomes conspicuous to the naked eye. Halley through history Before 1986, Halley had been seen and recorded on 29 occasions. In A.D. 66, observers described it as a sword in the skies above Jerusalem.

articles.body: Hydrogen may be the most common element in the cosmos, but scientists could use it to do something unique: uncover the nature of dark energy, the mysterious force driving the accelerating expansion of the universe. This new line of dark energy investigation comes from the fact that researchers have determined that the CHIME (Canadian Hydrogen Intensity Mapping Experiment) project can detect the faint radio glow of hydrogen from the universe's distant past. Not only does this represent a faster and much less expensive way to investigate dark energy, but it is a major milestone for CHIME. The instrument was specifically devised to investigate dark energy and its pervasive influence.

articles.title: SpaceX successfully launches 6,300 pounds of cargo to the International Space Station
articles.excerpt: SpaceX successfully launched more than 3 tons of cargo toward the International Space Station on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13).
articles.body: SpaceX launched its latest cargo mission to the International Space Station (ISS) on Tuesday morning (Oct. 13). A Falcon 9 rocket launched a robotic Dragon capsule to the orbiting lab from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station on Tuesday at 6:35 a.m. EDT (1035 GMT). The launch kicks off the CRS-35 mission, so named because it will be the 35th that SpaceX flies under a Commercial Resupply Services contract with NASA. A side by side view of a rocket engine in space and the interior of a rocket fairing containing cargo bound for the International Space Station. (Image credit: SpaceX, NASA) If all goes according to plan, Dragon will reach the International Space Station (ISS) on Thursday (Oct. 15), docking autonomously to the space-facing port of its Harmony module at around 11 a.m.
